stem: A nurse gently rolls and inverts a vial of NPH insulin before administration. After mixing, the insulin appears uniformly white and cloudy. How should the nurse interpret this finding?

options.A: This is the expected appearance of the NPH insulin suspension after proper resuspension
options.B: The insulin should be completely clear after mixing and must be warmed if cloudiness remains
options.C: Any uniformly white appearance proves contamination and requires automatic disposal
options.D: NPH insulin is a clear long-acting solution that should never require resuspension

rationale: HUMULIN N (NPH/isophane insulin) is a suspension. Its DailyMed instructions direct gentle rolling and inversion before use and state that it should look white and cloudy after mixing. A clear appearance, lumps, or particles are reasons not to use the product. A is correct.
educational_objective: Recognize the expected appearance and resuspension technique for NPH insulin before administration.
source_organization: DailyMed / U.S. National Library of Medicine (official FDA drug labeling)
source_document_title: HUMULIN N — insulin human injection, suspension
source_locator: Patient Instructions for Use — Preparing your HUMULIN N dose, Steps 1-2; Pen preparation Steps 2-4
source_claim_supported: HUMULIN N should be gently rolled and inverted to mix and should appear white and cloudy after mixing; do not use if clear or if lumps/particles are present.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication administration and client education
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — insulin administration

source_original.stem: A nurse is preparing to administer NPH insulin, which appears cloudy/uniformly white after gentle mixing. The nurse should recognize that:

options.A: An intermediate-acting insulin suspension that is normally cloudy after gentle resuspension
options.B: A clear insulin solution that should be warmed before injection whenever cloudiness develops
options.C: A contaminated insulin product that should always be discarded whenever it looks uniformly white
options.D: A long-acting insulin solution that should remain completely clear and never require mixing

source_original.rationale: NPH insulin is a suspension (intermediate-acting) and is normally cloudy/uniformly white after gentle mixing, unlike clear rapid- or long-acting insulins. It should be gently rolled between the hands or inverted (not shaken vigorously, which can cause bubbling and inaccurate dosing) to evenly resuspend the particles before drawing up the dose.
source_original.source_detail: DailyMed HUMULIN N instructions: white/cloudy suspension; gently roll and invert to resuspend; accessed 2026-08-14.

correction_summary: Kept the correct NPH appearance concept, tightened the stem to the labeled preparation sequence, and removed unsupported commentary about vigorous shaking causing inaccurate dosing. Added an exact DailyMed Instructions-for-Use locator.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current official DailyMed label; NCSBN 2026 blueprint
audit_findings.currentness: DailyMed HUMULIN N label and Instructions for Use were checked 2026-08-17.
audit_findings.claim_audit: The label directly supports gentle rolling/inversion and the expected white/cloudy appearance after mixing.

distractor_audit.B: Contradicts the labeled white/cloudy appearance and invents warming.
distractor_audit.C: Uniform white/cloudy appearance is expected after proper mixing; contamination is not inferred from that appearance alone.
distractor_audit.D: Misclassifies NPH as a clear long-acting solution.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: A is uniquely supported by the product label.
audit_findings.cueing: Stem gives only the clinically relevant preparation observation; choices remain parallel interpretations.
audit_findings.blueprint: Medication preparation and administration fits Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked vial and pen instructions; no second defensible answer identified.
